{"id": "W2789445850", "doi": "10.1136/bmjopen-2017-018815", "title": "Scoping review on the use of socially assistive robot technology in elderly care", "abstract": "OBJECTIVE: With an elderly population that is set to more than double by 2050 worldwide, there will be an increased demand for elderly care. This poses several impediments in the delivery of high-quality health and social care. Socially assistive robot (SAR) technology could assume new roles in health and social care to meet this higher demand. This review qualitatively examines the literature on the use of SAR in elderly care and aims to establish the roles this technology may play in the future. DESIGN: Scoping review. DATA SOURCES: Search of CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Embase, MEDLINE, PsychINFO and Scopus databases was conducted, complemented with a free search using Google Scholar and reference harvesting. All publications went through a selection process, which involved sequentially reviewing the title, abstract and full text of the publication. No limitations regarding date of publication were imposed, and only English publications were taken into account. The main search was conducted in March 2016, and the latest search was conducted in September 2017. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: The inclusion criteria consist of elderly participants, any elderly healthcare facility, humanoid and pet robots and all social interaction types with the robot. Exclusions were acceptability studies, technical reports of robots and publications surrounding physically or surgically assistive robots. RESULTS: In total, 61 final publications were included in the review, describing 33 studies and including 1574 participants and 11 robots. 28 of the 33 papers report positive findings. Five roles of SAR were identified: affective therapy, cognitive training, social facilitator, companionship and physiological therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Although many positive outcomes were reported, a large proportion of the studies have methodological issues, which limit the utility of the results. Nonetheless, the reported value of SAR in elderly care does warrant further investigation. Future studies should endeavour to validate the roles demonstrated in this review. # Social robots used with older people: a map of the empirical research

## Summary

- **Who is studied:** Mostly people with dementia living in nursing homes or long-term care.
- **Which robot:** PARO, the robotic seal, dominates. Other robots appear in only one or a few studies each.
- **What they found:** In the short term, results are fairly consistently positive for engagement, affect (observed emotional expression) and social interaction. Effects on clinical outcomes measured with standard scales (depression, agitation, cognition, quality of life) are mixed and often not statistically significant.
- **Evidence quality:** Reviews describe it as promising but weak: small samples, short trials, high risk of bias.
- **Where the gaps are:** Home studies, humanoid or conversational robots, and older adults without dementia are much less studied.

A note on scope: I searched until I hit the tool limit, so this map is wide but not exhaustive. I read the abstracts of the main studies; for some studies I only saw a search snippet, and I say so where that applies.

---

## 1. Start with these reviews

| Review | Scope | Bottom line |
|---|---|---|
| Pu et al. 2018, *Gerontologist* [W2808281222] | Meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (13 articles); 9 pooled | Positive trends for agitation, anxiety and quality of life, but none statistically significant when pooled. Narrative synthesis suggests gains in engagement, interaction and stress indicators, and less loneliness and medication use. High risk of bias in allocation concealment and blinding. |

## 3. Patterns across studies

1. **Settings:** Most studies are in nursing homes or long-term care, followed by dementia day care. Private-home studies are fewer, smaller and more technology-focused [W2994761079], [W2717439789].
2. **Populations:** Mostly moderate-to-severe dementia. There is less on older adults who are cognitively intact, depressed or lonely and living in the community.
3. **Outcomes:** Observed engagement, affect and social interaction improve fairly reliably [W2732925385], [W2955051104], [W1972564462]. Standardised scales for depression, quality of life, agitation and cognition often don't move [W2808281222], [W2955051104], [W1945345301]. Some exceptions:
   - sleep [W3088196398]
   - loneliness [W2132164645], [W3015603533]
   - apathy [W1807810766]
4. **Robots as social facilitators:** Several studies find robots spark interaction between people, not just with the robot [W2043711811], [W2732925385], [W3015603533].
5. **Responses vary a lot.** People respond very differently, and those with less impairment tend to benefit more [W2778691880], [W2732925385]. Novelty fades [W2294211165], [W1945345301].
6. **Comparison conditions matter.** Against a live dog or a plush toy, robots often perform similarly to the alternative, so the specific value of the robot is unclear [W2294211165], [W2132164645], [W2778691880].
7. **Methods:** Common weaknesses include small samples, short durations, no blinding, and developer-led studies [W2808281222], [W2789445850].
